title: Cu intercalation and field-driven filament formation in vertically aligned MoS$_2$ memristors
abstract: Vertically-aligned MoS$_2$ films paired with a Cu top electrode have been used as electrochemical metallization cell memristor devices. The memristive switching has been attributed to the formation of conductive filaments, yet their exact structure has remained elusive. Here we carry out a multi-scale computational study of Cu intercalation, clustering, and field-driven dynamics to eventually model the filament formation under operating conditions. We use density-functional theory results to fine-tune a machine learning force field, and the most important physical phenomena are further distilled into multi-particle kinetic Monte Carlo simulations. By exhaustive enumeration of Cu intercalated structures, we find the most stable structure at MoS$_2$Cu$_{0.11}$ composition, with Cu atoms forming a dice lattice between the MoS$_2$ layers. These structures are shown to exhibit metallic character and can thus form conductive filaments under memristor operation. The simulated switching speed and threshold voltage agree well with the available experimental data. Our results give fundamental insights on the device operation mechanism and guidelines for maximizing switching speed and endurance.
summary: This work computationally investigates how $	ext{Cu}$ intercalates into $	ext{MoS}_2$ memristors to form conductive filaments. By combining $	ext{DFT}$, $	ext{MLFF}$, and $	ext{kMC}$ simulations, the authors identified a stable, metallic $	ext{Cu}$-dice lattice structure. This provides fundamental insights into the resistive switching mechanism, validating the model against experimental device performance.
main_problem: To elucidate the atomic-scale mechanism governing conductive filament formation in $	ext{Cu}$-intercalated $	ext{MoS}_2$ memristors, as the exact filament structure is unknown.
main_result: The most stable structure is $	ext{MoS}_2	ext{Cu}_{0.11}$ featuring a metallic 'dice lattice' of $	ext{Cu}$ atoms, which is capable of forming conductive filaments under applied electric fields.
method: A multi-scale computational approach combining Density-Functional Theory ($	ext{DFT}$) for parameterization, Machine Learning Force Fields ($	ext{MLFF}$) for structure enumeration, and Kinetic Monte Carlo ($	ext{kMC}$) simulations for dynamic modeling.
model_or_system: The system is a vertically aligned $	ext{MoS}_2$ film with a $	ext{Cu}$ top electrode, modeled as an electrochemical metallization cell memristor. The simulation tracks $	ext{Cu}$ intercalation and subsequent field-driven atomic migration.
key_observables: Most stable $	ext{Cu}$ intercalated structure ($	ext{MoS}_2	ext{Cu}_{0.11}$), metallic character, simulated switching speed, and threshold voltage.
important_parameters: Electric field ($E$), temperature ($T$), $	ext{Cu}$ concentration (e.g., 11%), and calculated migration barriers ($E_a$).
main_assumptions: The $	ext{kMC}$ simulation uses a simplified model for the electric field and assumes constant attempt frequencies for $	ext{Cu}$ clusters due to computational constraints.
figures_summary: Figures benchmark $	ext{MLFF}$ accuracy against $	ext{DFT}$ and illustrate the atomic structure of the stable $	ext{Cu}$-dice lattice. Other figures detail the electronic structure and the $	ext{kMC}$ simulation setup showing field effects.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from benchmarking advanced ML potentials against DFT, to systematically searching for the global energy minimum structure ($	ext{Cu}$ intercalation), and finally applying $	ext{kMC}$ simulations incorporating external electric fields to model the dynamic filament formation.
why_interesting: The use of $	ext{kMC}$ simulations to model non-equilibrium, field-driven processes in solid-state devices is a sophisticated application of computational physics, bridging quantum mechanical inputs ($	ext{DFT}$) to macroscopic device behavior.

FIG. 2: Cu clustering structure search. a MLFF calculated binding energies Eb per Cu of 14715 unique structures with their Cu concentrations. The DFT results of the most favorable structures (7.7%, 10.0%, 11.1%, 12.2%) are marked in with black crosses. b Atomic structures of the lowest energy systems and their DFT binding energies. The upper MoS2 layer has been removed to better illustrate the Cu structure within the vdW gap. c Binding energies and atomic structures of MoS2Cu0.11 with differently filled vdW gaps.

FIG. 3: Electronic structure of Cu-dice sublattice. a Electron localization of Cu-dice sublattice from side view as well as horizontal 2D slices from the indicated locations resulting in the Cu sublattice shown on the right. Electronic band structure and PDOS of b 2×2 2H-MoS2 and c Cu-dice MoS2 with the Fermi levels marked with dashed lines. d Charge density and Bader charge difference of Cu-dice vs. pristine MoS2 and free Cu. Green represents loss of electron charge density while red indicates gain. The Bader charges for the associated layers are marked on the side of the figure.

FIG. 4: Dimer expansion and benchmarking against FT-MLFF. a Dimer binding energy per Cu distance. Site combinations are indicated with different colors. b Comparison of the dimer expansion and FT-MLFF calculated binding energies (per Cu) of randomly generated clusters containing four Cu atoms.

FIG. 5: Cu-dice cluster formation and breakdown. a-d Resulting clusters from running kMC at room temperature starting from a random Cu allocation corresponding to the indicated Cu concentrations. Distances and triangle configurations corresponding to the Cu-dice clusters are marked in with purple for clarity. e The structures as well as the amount of Cu-dice triangular configurations with different temperatures starting from a random Cu-6% allocation in the simulation box.
